t.2.20.1: But as Rāma was speaking thus, Lakṣmaṇa, hearing him, his head bowed low again and again, went, as it were, in his mind to a point midway between sorrow and joy.
t.2.20.2: Then that bull among men, knitting a frown between his brows, hissed like a great serpent enraged in its hole.
t.2.20.3: Then his face, knitted with a frown and hard to look upon, shone like the face of an enraged lion.
t.2.20.4: Shaking it as an untamed elephant shakes its own trunk, and tossing his neck sideways and upward upon his body,
t.2.20.5: Glancing sidelong at his brother out of the corner of his eye, he said: “You, in whom this very great agitation has arisen, and that without due cause…”
t.2.20.6: How can one such as you, free of agitation, bring yourself to say this, through concern over a lapse in dharma and so as not to arouse the misgivings of the people?
t.2.20.7: Though you yourself are heroic, a bull among kṣatriyas, you speak of fate, which has no heroism in it. Why do you extol fate, that wretched and powerless thing?
t.2.20.8: How is it that you have no suspicion of those two wicked ones? There are smooth-tongued people who use dharma as a cloak for deceit; O righteous one, why do you not perceive this?
t.2.20.9: The consecration of someone other than you, a thing the people abhor, has been set in motion, and because of it this mind of yours, O lord of the earth, has become divided. Hateful to me indeed is that dharma through attachment to which you are so bewildered.
t.2.20.10: Even if your conviction is that this is the work of fate, and this is also the view of those two, still you ought to disregard it; that too does not please me.
t.2.20.11: He who is faint-hearted and devoid of valor submits to fate; heroes who hold themselves in high esteem do not bow down before fate.
t.2.20.12: The man who is able to overpower fate by his own effort does not lose heart, even when his purposes have been thwarted by fate.
t.2.20.13: But today they will see the might of fate and the might of man; today the difference between fate and human effort will become plainly manifest.
t.2.20.14: Today the people shall indeed see fate struck down by my manly might, since today they have seen your royal consecration struck down by fate.
t.2.20.16: Not all those guardians of the worlds together, nor even the three worlds in their entirety, could obstruct Rāma's consecration today, how much less his father!
t.2.20.15: As one turns back a charging elephant, defiant of the goad, unrestrained and maddened by the force of its rut, so I will turn back fate by my own manly prowess.
t.2.20.17: Those who together contrived your exile to the forest, O king, shall themselves dwell in the forest for fourteen years in the same way.
t.2.20.18: I shall cut off that hope of your father and of her, which, through the obstruction of your consecration, is bent upon the kingdom for her son.
t.2.20.19: For one who stands opposed by my might, the power of fate will not bring such sorrow as my fierce manly valor will.
t.2.20.20: Later, at the end of a thousand years, when you have gone to dwell in the forest, the noble one's sons will then take up the protection of the people.
t.2.20.21: For according to the conduct of the royal sages of old, dwelling in the forest is prescribed once one has entrusted one's subjects to one's sons for their protection, as though they were one's own children.
t.2.20.22: If, O righteous-souled Rāma, you do not wish the kingdom for yourself in this way because you fear turmoil in the realm while the king's mind is wavering...
t.2.20.23: And I swear to you, O hero, and may I never share in the world of heroes if I fail: I shall guard your kingdom as the shore guards the ocean.
t.2.20.24: Have yourself consecrated with the auspicious rites, and be devoted to that task. I alone am able to hold back the kings by force.
t.2.20.25: These two arms of mine are not for beauty, nor is my bow for ornament; my sword is not merely for wearing at the waist, nor are my arrows meant to stand idle like posts.
t.2.20.26: All these four of mine are meant for subduing enemies, and I have no great liking for anyone who would be regarded as my enemy.
t.2.20.27: With my sword grasped firmly in hand, its edge keen and its brilliance flashing like lightning, I would count no enemy as anything, not even the wielder of the thunderbolt himself.
t.2.20.28: Through me the earth will become dense and impassable, strewn with the hands and great heads of elephants, horses and men crushed by the blows of my sword.
t.2.20.29: Struck down today by the edge of my sword, elephants like blazing mountains will fall to the ground, like clouds flashing with lightning.
t.2.20.31: Striking down one man with many arrows and many men with a single arrow, I shall drive my shafts into the vital parts of men, horses and elephants.
t.2.20.30: While I stand here with my leather finger-guards fastened and my bow grasped in hand, how could anyone among men think himself a man?
t.2.20.32: Today the might of me, whose strength lies in my weapons, will prevail, to render the king powerless and to establish your lordship, O lord.
t.2.20.33: Today, for these arms that are worthy of the finest sandalwood paste and the fastening on of armlets, of the giving away of riches and the protection of friends…
t.2.20.34: O Rāma, these two arms, fit for the task, will accomplish the work of holding back those who would obstruct your consecration.
t.2.20.35: Tell me, which enemy of yours is to be parted by me this very day from his life, his fame and his friends? Command me so that this earth may come under your sway; I am your servant.
t.2.20.36: Wiping away his tears and consoling Lakṣmaṇa again and again, he who prospers the line of the Rāghavas said: "Know that I stand firm in my father's word, for this, gentle one, is the path of the good."
